planting.note: Transplant nursery-propagated divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich, acidic soil under dense shade, and avoid disturbing the shallow rhizomes once established.

directions: Hexastylis lewisii is a Piedmont endemic of the Carolinas and Georgia, forming a slow-spreading evergreen mat of glossy, heart-shaped leaves that stay attractive through winter in mild climates. Plant divisions in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic soil beneath hardwood canopy, matching the deep leaf-litter conditions of its native forests. Inconspicuous brownish-purple jug-shaped flowers open at ground level in early spring and are pollinated by fungus gnats and other ground-dwelling insects. Growth is slow, so give plants several seasons before expecting full groundcover coverage, and source only nursery-propagated stock since wild populations are limited and locally uncommon.

planting.note: Divide established clumps in early fall and reset into cool, moist, acidic soil in deep mountain-forest-style shade, keeping the rhizomes shallow and undisturbed afterward.

directions: Native to a narrow range along the French Broad River drainage in the southern Appalachians, this rare heartleaf forms a tight, low mat of leathery, rhombic-shaped evergreen leaves suited to cool, humid mountain woodlands. Grow it in consistently moist, cool, humus-rich acidic soil beneath a closed hardwood canopy, and avoid summer heat and drying winds by siting it in a sheltered ravine-like microclimate if gardening outside its native mountain range. Like its relatives, it produces small brown urn-shaped flowers hidden at soil level in spring, pollinated by ground-active insects rather than typical pollinators. Because this species has a very restricted native distribution and conservation concern, plant only nursery-propagated material and never dig from the wild.
